The course at a glance

The twenty-one bottles at home differ in how much they assert. Six say everything they have to say on their own, seven leave room, and seven have never been rated. Layering is the question of what goes into the room the quiet ones leave, and each lesson isolates one variable of that question.

17 wearing days5 modulesone variable per lessonpredict before you spray
How to smell, before any of this works

When you stop smelling your own wrist, the scent is still there. Recordings taken directly at the olfactory epithelium show the receptor signal holding steady across repeated exposures while people's intensity ratings fall; the drop happens in the cortex, not in the nose (Mignot et al. 2021). Two weeks of living with one odour raised detection thresholds that were still measurable two weeks after it stopped (Dalton and Wysocki 1996). So after roughly half an hour on your own skin, your report is of your attention, not of the perfume. Someone who walks into the room is better instrumentation, and so is a sleeve you sprayed and left.

Coffee beans do nothing. In the one controlled test, sniffing coffee between perfumes produced 62 percent correct identification against 57 percent for plain air, a difference that did not reach significance (Grosofsky et al. 2011). Smelling the crook of your elbow or a wool sleeve is untested either way: plausible, never measured. What is measured is removal and time. And wearing a perfume of your own while trying to judge another one lowers your combined smell-test score from 33 to 27 (Beekman et al. 2022), which is why every lesson here starts with clean skin and nothing else on it.

A perfume does not evaporate in three stages. Everything leaves at once, at different speeds. Measured on forearms over seven hours, linalool was 68 percent gone and cinnamic alcohol 4 percent gone, although cinnamic alcohol is the lighter molecule; what governs the rate is vapour pressure, not weight (Saiyasombati and Kasting 2003). The top, heart and base pyramid descends from Poucher's 1 to 100 evaporation coefficients and Jean Carles's three columns, and the timings usually quoted for each tier carry, on their most-read summary, a literal citation needed. Turin still uses the three stages descriptively, so treat it as a working sketch of one continuous curve. The clock table in every lesson is about when you read, not about tiers.

Skin, paper and cloth are three different instruments. Skin runs at about 34 degrees, carries sebum that dissolves the oil-loving materials, and hosts bacteria that transform some of them; a blotter does none of that, which is why Sylvaine Delacourte calls paper one-dimensional and skin three-dimensional. Cloth holds a scent for days because it has none of the skin's heat or chemistry; that is an inference from textile science rather than a fragrance study, and the course uses it as one. Where a lesson wants a stable reading, it asks for cloth; where it wants the real thing, skin.

A nose is a memory, not an organ. Carles, who trained Grasse's perfumers for decades, wrote that anyone may acquire a highly developed sense of smell as this is merely a matter of practice, and set aside half an hour a day for it; a working perfumer interviewed sixty years later says I do not believe I have a better sense of smell than the average person. Speakers of Jahai name odours as readily as colours, because their language has words for them (Majid and Burenhult 2014). But one thing to hold onto: a controlled study found that giving people the names of what they were smelling changed how they described it and not at all how well they could tell two samples apart (Cormiea and Fischer 2023). Naming and discriminating are separate skills. The course trains both, and does not pretend one is the other.

Compare, and predict before you smell. Two things side by side on two forearms are far easier to tell apart than one thing on its own; every professional method from Carles's ratio pairs to a factory's retained reference batch is built on judging against an anchor rather than in isolation. Smell A, then B, then A again before you write anything. And write the prediction before the spray, because expectation overrides even trained noses: 54 oenology students described a white wine dyed red in the vocabulary of red wine (Morrot et al. 2001). Where a lesson can be run blind, with a second person spraying the arms and not telling you which is which, it says so.

Nothing is layered yet. These four establish what your nose does over a day, what a single material sounds like, and whether you can perceive the two commonest fixatives at all, so that every later result is readable rather than a mood.

One bottleA full dayCalibration

Rate the one you never rated

The sheet carries a comment on this bottle but no verdict, so it is the one whose class nothing in your record decides. A full day, read at fixed times, settles it and installs the habit every later lesson runs on.

1 bottle6 h of readings1 second nose
A

Before you start

  • Moonlark Ash, two sprays on the inside of one forearm, from about ten centimetres. Nothing else on the skin that day: no other perfume, no scented soap or lotion that morning.
  • Alarms at 0:30, 2:00 and 6:00. Not reminders you might notice; alarms.
  • A second person around hour three. Someone you live with is the obvious one.
  • Somewhere to write four short readings. Section D below, or paper you will copy in.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:00Alcohol and the lightest materials, loud and unrepresentative.Nothing. Do not write yet.
0:30The opening has mostly gone; the bergamot and pepper are giving way to the pine and sap.One line: what is it doing now, in plain words.
2:00The heart, warmed by skin. Your nose has been adapting for ninety minutes.One line. Does it still say what it said at 0:30?
3:00You are now reporting your attention, not the perfume.Ask your second nose. Write what they say, not what you think.
6:00Base only, close to the skin: cypress, vetiver, incense, whatever is left.One line. Then the verdict: complete, open, or strong.
C

Steps

1
Two sprays, one forearm, then leave it alone

Spray Moonlark Ash twice on the inside of one forearm and let it dry on its own. Do not rub the wrists together.

Why not rubRubbing spreads the liquid thin and warms it, which pushes the most volatile materials off faster and changes the opening. Since the opening is the part of the day you are about to ignore anyway, the damage is small, but the habit is worth breaking now.
Watch for: The first ten minutesAlcohol and top notes. Whatever you think of it in this window is a judgment on the part that is leaving.
2
Read at the alarm, not when you remember
0:30

At each alarm, smell the forearm from a normal distance first, then close. Write one line. Then stop smelling it until the next alarm.

Why the clock beats attentionAttention is drawn by intensity. An unscheduled reading over-samples the loud moments and under-samples the drydown, which is most of the day. Fixed times catch the quiet hours, and they make readings comparable across lessons: 0:30 here means the same thing as 0:30 in lesson 12.
Watch for: Checking between alarmsEach sniff between readings adds to the adaptation you are trying to read around. Leave it.
3
Borrow a nose at hour three
3:00

Ask your second nose what it smells like from a normal distance, and whether they can still smell it at all. Write down their words.

Why hour threeBy then your cortex has been suppressing the report for over two hours; the receptor signal has not changed (Mignot et al. 2021). Someone who walks into the room has none of that history and is reading the perfume, not your attention.
Watch for: Leading the witnessAsk what it smells like, not whether it smells of campfire. The description you want is hers.
4
The verdict at six hours
6:00

Write the last line, then decide: does this bottle say everything it has to say on its own, does it leave room, or does it set the terms of whatever it is in? That is the sheet's missing verdict. Put it in the sheet as well; the course is built from it.

Nothing is decided in the first ten minutes

A complete bottle on one arm and an open one on the other, read at the same clock times. The point is to watch two evaporation curves diverge, and to see how little the opening predicted about either.

2 bottles2 forearms4 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Trudon II on the left forearm, Bois d Ebene on the right. Two sprays each, same distance, within a minute of each other so the clocks line up.
  • Alarms at 0:10, 1:00 and 4:00.
  • Optional and better: a second person sprays the arms and does not tell you which is which. You find out at hour four.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:10Both openings. Alcohol gone, the most volatile materials still loud: green leaves and bitter orange on one arm, juniper on the other.One word for each arm.
1:00Hearts. Cedar and pepper against palo santo. The complete one should still read from arm's length.One line each, and which is louder.
4:00Drydowns. Incense and ambroxan against patchouli and cypriol. This is the reading the lesson exists for.Which is still legible? What is left of each? If run blind, now guess which is which.
C

Steps

1
Both arms, same amount, same minute

Trudon II left, Bois d Ebene right, two sprays each.

Watch for: Cross-contaminationKeep the wrists apart for the first hour. Crossed arms on a desk is how two experiments become one.
2
Smell A, then B, then A again

At each clock time, smell the left arm, then the right, then the left again, before writing. The second pass at A is where the difference shows.

Why comparison beats judgmentDiscrimination and identification run on different memory systems: telling two things apart uses working memory and is fast; naming one thing alone uses long-term semantic memory and is slow (Royet et al. 2013). Every professional method, from Carles's ratio pairs to a factory's retained reference batch, judges against an anchor rather than in isolation. Coming back to A after B makes A's character stand out against B in a way one sniff of A never does.
Watch for: The adapted noseBy hour four you are adapted to both. Smell a clean patch of skin, or the inside of your sleeve, for ten seconds between arms. That is untested folklore as a reset, but it costs nothing; coffee beans are tested and do nothing (Grosofsky et al. 2011).
3
The four-hour reading
4:00

Write which arm is still legible from a normal distance and what is left of it. Compare to your 0:10 words. How much of what you wrote at ten minutes survived?

Why the opening liesMeasured on skin, everything is evaporating from minute zero at its own rate, set by vapour pressure rather than by weight: over seven hours linalool was 68 percent gone and cinnamic alcohol 4 percent gone, although the second is the lighter molecule (Saiyasombati and Kasting 2003). The opening is whatever has the highest vapour pressure, which is also whatever is gone first. Judging a perfume at ten minutes is judging the part that is leaving.
4
If you ran it blind, reveal now

Ask your second nose which arm was which. If you guessed wrong, that is the most useful result of the day: it means the drydowns had converged enough that the names in your head, not the smell on your arm, were doing the work.

Why blind mattersExpectation overrides even trained noses. Given a white wine dyed red, 54 oenology students described it in the vocabulary of red wine (Morrot et al. 2001). Labels change what you say about a smell; they do not change what you can discriminate (Cormiea and Fischer 2023). Running blind protects the description.

Two bottlesBoth forearmsCalibration

One idea, loudly

Two compositions that are each close to a single idea, so you can hear what one material does before you have to find it inside something that is not about it. This is the scales exercise, and Carles said perfumers should practise scales like concert pianists.

2 bottles1 word each4 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Vetiver 46 on one forearm: smoky vetiver with olibanum and pepper.
  • Wonderwood on the other: a wood overdose of cedar, cypress, guaiac and sandalwood.
  • A word budget of one per arm per reading. Not a sentence.
  • For step 3, after the four-hour reading: Moonlark Ash, Victrix, Trudon II or Fuego Futuro to hand, all of which carry vetiver or cedar in the base.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Both are past the opening. On one arm the vetiver has arrived; on the other the cypress and cedar.One word for each. Not a sentence.
2:00Both hearts. The olibanum is showing on one arm; the guaiac on the other.One word again. Same word as 0:30?
4:00Drydowns. Labdanum and amber under the vetiver; sandalwood and patchouli under the cedar.One word. Then step 3.
C

Steps

1
One word, not a description

At each clock time, write one word for each arm. If you cannot get it to one word, you have not found the idea yet; wait a minute on clean skin and smell again.

Why one wordA specific name is what makes a material findable later. People given a specific name for an odour recalled it correctly around 80 to 90 percent of the time; a vague one dropped that to about half (Cain, as reported in the identification literature). Describing in a sentence feels like understanding and leaves nothing you can recognise next week inside another bottle.
Watch for: Borrowing the marketing noteSmoky, woody and dry are the words on the box. Aim for a word that is yours: burnt rope, pencil shavings, church, sauna bench. Precision, not poetry.
2
Same word at four hours?
4:00

Compare the three words per arm. If they changed, the material you named at 0:30 was not the dominant one; it was the loudest one at that moment.

Why the word driftsDifferent materials habituate at different rates, and the rate is set by their volatility and potency rather than their family (Sinding et al. 2017). The one you can still name at four hours is the one that is actually running the composition.
3
Find the same material somewhere else

After the four-hour reading, spray one of Moonlark Ash, Victrix, Trudon II or Fuego Futuro on the back of a hand and look for the word you wrote. Vetiver is in the base of the first two; cedar in the last two.

Why this is the whole methodNaming a material alone and then finding it inside a composition is how noses are trained at Givaudan, where first-year students memorise roughly five hundred materials in four to seven months and then spend a year on how they combine (Nez). You are doing the same thing with two materials and a small shelf.
Watch for: Expecting it to be obviousInside a composition the same material is a tenth as loud and surrounded. You are listening for a shape, not a volume. If you cannot find it, smell the reference arm again and go back; the pair, A then B then A, is the tool.

At IngredientsTwo moleculesCalibration

Can you smell Iso E Super at all

Molecule 01 is Iso E Super alone; Molecule 02 is ambroxan alone, which is already in the base of Trudon II. One arm each. The result can close a route rather than open one, and that is why it is here early.

1 shop visit2 single molecules1 h minimum, outside
A

Before you start

  • Nothing else on your skin that morning. No scented soap, no other perfume. Your own perfume measurably lowers your ability to smell anything else (Beekman et al. 2022).
  • Ingredients, Vezenska 4. Ask for Molecule 01 on one forearm and Molecule 02 on the other.
  • An hour of not buying anything, most of it outside the shop.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:05Both are quiet by design. Read this on the street, not in the shop.Can you smell each at all? Yes, faint, or no.
1:00Iso E Super is reported to come and go on some people; ambroxan tends to sit.Same three-way answer, both arms. Then the fork.
C

Steps

1
Spray, then walk out

Get both on, then leave. Read them on the street at five minutes and somewhere calm at an hour.

Watch for: Reading it in the shopEverything in the room is louder than what is on your arm. The five-minute reading is outside or it is worthless.
2
Three answers, not a description

For each arm at each time: yes, faint, or no. This is a test of your receptors, not of your taste.

Why this is a test of youSpecific anosmia, being unable to smell one particular material while smelling everything else normally, is common, inherited and molecule-specific. For musks it has been known since 1973, when about one in twelve subjects tested could not smell exaltolide (Whissell-Buechy and Amoore, Nature). The share of people blind to Iso E Super is widely quoted at about a fifth, but that figure circulates in industry blogs without a traceable study behind it; treat it as folklore with a real phenomenon underneath. Two things from 2025 are not folklore. The receptor for Iso E Super's active isomer has been identified as OR7A17 (Emter et al., Current Biology), and the receptor for ambroxan has been identified as OR7A17 as well (Takase et al., Communications Biology), with non-functional versions of it common in some populations. So your two arms may be one test, not two: if 01 is nothing on you, read 02 closely, and if 02 is fine, Trudon II's base explains itself. And in a laboratory test of repeated exposure, Iso E Super was the one odorant whose rated intensity did not decline (Mignot et al. 2021). Its maker describes it coming and going over minutes to an hour on the same person; that is his account, not a measurement. If it vanishes for you entirely, that is your receptors, not adaptation.
Watch for: Calling faint a noFaint is an answer. Iso E Super is faint on nearly everyone who can smell it; that is the whole point of it.
3
What a fixative does, in one sentence

If you can smell either, notice that it has almost no character. That absence is the tool.

Why a near-odourless molecule is useful, and the dissentA fixative lowers the overall vapour pressure of a mixture and slows the volatile materials down. On skin, a musk fixative measurably depressed the early evaporation of the most volatile top notes, linalool and limonene, and released them later (Saiyasombati and Kasting 2003). So a fixative does not just make the base last; it makes the opening last. Trudon II runs on ambroxan and cashmeran in the base for that reason. Two dissents are worth keeping. Jellinek, co-author of the standard perfumery textbook, is reported to have concluded that fixatives work on a blotter and cannot be expected to do much in ordinary wear; that is a secondhand quote, but from the right person. And an experienced Basenotes poster argues that adding ambroxan to another perfume only increases the projection of ambroxan, so what reads as a boost is two clouds overlapping. The measurement on skin is the stronger evidence, but lesson 13 lets you check the dissent on your own wrist.
D

Prediction, then result

Where this splits. The result decides which branch you are on.

One wayIf 01 reads as nothing on you, the universal-blender route is shut. Read 02 carefully before assuming ambroxan is fine, since the two may share a receptor; if 02 is clear, every fixative move later runs on it and you already wear it daily.
The otherIf it reads clearly, you have a tool that adds body and time without adding a smell, and the open question becomes whether a pure synthetic belongs in a collection you built on the opposite principle. Your daily bottle's base suggests it already does.

Two zonesTwo greensOpen under complete

Two things that agree

Moss on one patch of skin, Trudon II on another nearby, sharing the air. Both are green and mossy, so most of what they contain is the same thing said twice, and the lesson is what that does.

2 bottles2 zones4 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Moss, one spray on the inside of the left wrist. Trudon II, one spray on the left forearm a hand's width above it. Two zones, one arm, sharing the air.
  • Trudon II alone, one spray, on the right forearm. This is the control.
  • One spray each, not two. When you combine, halve the dose.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Two openings sharing the air: green leaves and grapefruit against pine and bitter orange.Louder, or different? Compare the pair arm to the control arm.
2:00Two hearts that overlap: cedar, pine and pepper on both.Name one thing gained, one thing lost, against the control.
4:00Drydowns merged in the air: oakmoss and musk under incense and ambroxan.Would you wear the pair over Trudon II alone?
C

Steps

1
Two zones, not one spot

Moss on the wrist, Trudon II a hand's width up the same arm. They never touch the same skin; they mix in the air above it.

Why not the same spotThe commercial advice is to spray one over the other. The practitioners who have actually tested it say otherwise: a perfumer at CaFleureBon recommends applying at different locations and letting the fragrances commingle in the air, and Parfumo users who ran the same pair both ways found the same-spot version cancelled notes, especially citrus, while side by side blended. The mechanism is plausible: on one spot the second spray partly dissolves and covers the first, so you get one evaporation curve sitting on top of another rather than two beside each other. Lesson 7 tests this directly. Until then, zones.
Watch for: Zones too far apartA wrist and an elbow is two perfumes. A wrist and a hand's width up is one cloud.
2
One spray each

Halve the dose when you combine.

Why halveA Basenotes thread on whether layering is a myth lands on the obvious point: people notice increased performance when layering because they are wearing twice as much perfume. Two sprays of each is four sprays. Keep the total constant and the comparison to the control arm is honest.
3
Trudon II alone on the other arm

One spray of Trudon II on the right forearm at the same time. Pair on the left, control on the right.

Watch for: Skipping the controlWithout Trudon II alone beside it, louder and better are indistinguishable. Louder is the expected result here.
4
Gain and loss, in writing
2:00

Name one thing the pair has that Trudon II alone does not, and one thing it has lost. If you cannot name a gain, that is the finding.

Why this pair is in the courseOverlapping materials add concentration rather than a dimension. Moss and Trudon II share cedar, pine, pepper and a green top; the pair is mostly the same idea at a higher dose. Perfumers interviewed about layering say the same from the other side: if a perfume is already complex, layering another on top becomes overwhelming, and simple single-theme compositions benefit most (CaFleureBon 2021). Finding the words for louder versus deeper now is what makes the later pairs readable.
D

Prediction, then result

Two zonesDifferent jobsOpen under complete

Powder under smoke

Dry powdery wood on the wrist, smoke and hay a hand's width above. The first pair where the two bottles are doing different jobs instead of the same job twice, and the first that should read as deeper rather than louder.

2 bottles2 roles6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Bois d Ebene, one spray on the left wrist. Fuego Futuro, one spray a hand's width up the left forearm.
  • Fuego Futuro alone, one spray, on the right forearm as the control.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Fuego's elemi, mate and pepper in the air above the juniper of the base.Does the powder show yet, or is it all Fuego?
2:00Smoke, hay and sage; palo santo and guaiac underneath.Texture, or dilution? Compare to the control arm.
6:00Ash, cedar and sandalwood with patchouli and cypriol.Gain, loss, and would you wear the pair over Fuego Futuro alone?
C

Steps

1
Powder down, smoke above

Bois d Ebene on the wrist, Fuego Futuro above it. The powdery one is a surface rather than a smell, which is why it can sit near a loud one without arguing with it.

Why powder does not arguePowdery materials read as a texture rather than a note: they change how a scent feels without adding a competing idea. That is what a base is for. This is the pair the perfumers' rule predicts should work: one simple, one complex, different jobs (CaFleureBon 2021).
2
Read for texture at two hours
2:00

Ask one question: does the powder read as texture under the smoke, or as dilution of it? Those are the two outcomes and they feel different.

Why the distinction mattersDilution is what you get when the base has nothing of its own to contribute; the top bottle is simply quieter. Texture is what you get when the base has a surface: the top bottle is the same volume and a different shape. Smell the control arm between passes; the difference is only visible against it.
Watch for: Calling dilution smoothA pair that is merely quieter than the top bottle alone has been diluted. Smooth is a texture you can point to; quieter is a volume.
3
Six hours: who is left
6:00

By now the elemi and mate are long gone and the two drydowns are what remain: ash and cedar from one, patchouli and cypriol from the other. Is that one thing or two?

Why six hours is a different questionThe two bottles have different vapour-pressure profiles, so the pair at six hours is a different pair from the one at two. A layering can work at one clock time and not another; the honest verdict says which.
D

Prediction, then result

Sources
  • Perfumer workshop: layering natural fragrances, part 1, CaFleureBon, June 2021
  • Saiyasombati and Kasting, Two-stage kinetic analysis of fragrance evaporation and absorption from skin, Int J Cosmetic Science 2003
Three placementsOne dayOpen under complete

Order and distance

The same pair as the last lesson, three ways at once: on the same spot, in two zones, and split between cloth and skin. Three variables people collapse into one, run side by side so you never confuse them again.

2 bottles3 placements6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Left forearm, same spot: Bois d Ebene first, then Fuego Futuro directly over it a minute later.
  • Right forearm, two zones: Bois d Ebene on the wrist, Fuego Futuro a hand's width up, as in lesson 6.
  • Shirt cuff: Bois d Ebene on the fabric, Fuego Futuro on the skin just below it. They never touch.
  • One spray of each per placement. Six sprays in total, which is a lot; do this on a day at home.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Three openings. The same-spot arm should read as one thing; the zoned arm as a cloud.Which arm is louder? Which is more Fuego? Which is more Bois?
2:00The placement should show by now.Left versus right: what is different? Cloth versus skin: what is different?
6:00Cloth still holds; skin has warmed and metabolised.Which of the three would you still wear?
C

Steps

1
Same spot on the left

Bois d Ebene on the skin, wait a minute, Fuego Futuro directly over it.

Why order shows on one spotThe second spray lands on a surface already wet with the first and partly dissolves into it, so it meets the air first and covers what is underneath. Practitioners report that the last one sprayed usually overpowers the other (Basenotes) and that same-spot stacking cancels notes rather than blending them (Parfumo). You are checking that on your own skin.
2
Two zones on the right

Bois d Ebene on the wrist, Fuego Futuro above it. This is lesson 6 again, as the reference.

3
Cloth and skin at the cuff

Bois d Ebene on the shirt cuff, Fuego Futuro on the skin just under it.

Why cloth is a different instrumentCloth has none of the skin's heat, sebum or bacteria, so the scent on it stays closer to what is in the bottle and lasts longer; that is an inference from textile science, not a fragrance study, and it is treated as one here. Skin at 34 degrees drives the volatile materials off faster and its lipids hold the oil-loving ones (Saiyasombati and Kasting 2003). Delacourte calls paper one-dimensional and skin three-dimensional; cloth sits between.
4
Write the three-way verdict at two hours
2:00

Three lines: what the same-spot version is, what the zoned version is, what the cuff version is. Then which you would wear at six.

Watch for: Six sprays on one bodyYou are adapted to all of it by hour two. Ask your second nose to read the three placements from a normal distance. This is the lesson where a second nose matters most.
D

Prediction, then result

Two quiet ones

Petrichor Plains on the wrist, Citrus Batikanga above it. Rain, iris and violet against chilli, rhubarb and cardamom. Neither says much alone, and there is no complete bottle to lean on, so the result is entirely the pair's.

2 bottles0 complete ones6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Petrichor Plains, one spray on the left wrist. Citrus Batikanga, one spray a hand's width up the left forearm.
  • Nothing on the right arm. There is no complete bottle here to control against; your memory of each alone from earlier wearings is the control.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Bergamot and cardamom in the air over rain and iris.Is there a shape yet, or two smells?
2:00Chilli and rhubarb over violet and rosemary.Does the spice give the rain a shape, or sit on it?
6:00Vetiver, myrrh and fenugreek over amyris and buddawood.Gain, loss, and would you wear it?
C

Steps

1
The quiet base

Petrichor Plains on the wrist. It has body and no strong direction of its own, which is what a base is for.

Why Petrichor PlainsIris and cardamom run through several bottles you rated lower and through none you rated highly, which is worth knowing before you read this pair. But the bottle has weight without an argument, and that is the property being used. Perfumers put it the other way: simple compositions layer well; complex ones fight (CaFleureBon 2021).
2
Spice above it

Citrus Batikanga a hand's width up. The spice is the statement; the rain is the room it is in.

Watch for: Two perfumes side by sideIf at two hours you can smell two things rather than one, they have not merged. Write that. It is the commonest result in layering and it is informative: it usually means the two share no material to meet on.
3
Six hours: the drydowns meet or they do not
6:00

Vetiver from one, amyris from the other. Both are woody, both are quiet. This is the reading most likely to have merged, because the loud, fast materials that kept them apart are gone.

Why late merges happenThe materials that make two perfumes read as two are the volatile ones, each with a strong character of its own. Once they have evaporated, what is left is base materials, which are fewer, slower and more alike across perfumes. A pair that reads as two at 0:30 and one at 6:00 is normal, and the honest verdict names the hour.
D

Prediction, then result

Rain and turpentine

Wet mineral on the wrist, sharp coniferous camphor above. Both leave room, but in different places: one is diffuse, the other is narrow. The lesson is learning to tell those two kinds of open apart.

2 bottles2 directions6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Petrichor Plains, one spray on the left wrist. Monocle scent One: Hinoki, one spray a hand's width up.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Turpentine and thyme in the air over rain.Sharp over soft, or just sharp?
2:00Cypress, camphor and vetiver over violet and rosemary.Same direction, or different? Decide this before deciding whether you like it.
6:00Moss and frankincense over sandalwood.Gain, loss, wear it?
C

Steps

1
Name the direction before the verdict
2:00

At two hours, before you decide whether you like it, decide which case this is: open in the same direction, so they thin each other, or in different ones, so they build.

Why direction comes firstOpen is not one property. A diffuse bottle leaves room everywhere; a narrow one leaves room on both sides of a single line. Two narrow bottles on different lines can build; two diffuse ones cannot, they only dilute. Petrichor Plains is diffuse. Hinoki is narrow. If this pair builds, it is because the narrow one drew a line through the diffuse one. Liking comes after that diagnosis, or it tells you nothing you can reuse.
2
Where the camphor goes

Camphor and turpentine are high vapour pressure; they will be gone by hour two. What does the pair look like without them?

Why this pair changes fastHinoki's character is carried by its most volatile materials, which is why you called it boring: the interesting part leaves in the first hour and the drydown is a plain conifer wood. Over Petrichor Plains, that first hour is the whole experiment; after it you are wearing a different pair.
Watch for: Judging at six hours onlyThis is the one pair in the course where the 0:30 reading is the important one. Do not skip it.
D

White flower over amber

Amber and smoke on the wrist, orange blossom above. One of the oldest moves in perfumery, and it works because the two are doing different jobs on different clocks rather than because they suit each other. Day two tries it as a relay.

2 bottles2 days1 classic move

A borrowed Eau de Sens works here too and you rate the two about equally, so take whichever the day suggests and note which one you reached for.

A

Before you start

  • Day one, simultaneous: V Amber Fouguere, one spray on the left wrist. Fleur d'Oranger 27, one spray a hand's width up, a minute later.
  • Day two, relay: V Amber Fouguere alone in the morning, one spray on the left wrist. At hour three, Fleur d'Oranger 27 one spray a hand's width up, onto the amber's drydown.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Day one: orange blossom and petitgrain in the air over black pepper and bergamot.Which is on top? Obvious, but write it.
3:00Day one: the blossom fading into frankincense and amber. Day two: this is when the blossom goes on.Day one: which dominates now? Day two: what does fresh blossom do to a three-hour amber?
6:00Vetiver, smoke and amber with whatever the blossom left.Both days: gain, loss, wear it? Then compare the two days.
C

Steps

1
Day one: heavy on the wrist, light above

V Amber Fouguere first, Fleur d'Oranger 27 a minute later. The amber is heavier and slower; the blossom is lighter and faster. Put the slow one where it will be met last.

Why this pairing is oldA high vapour pressure floral over a low vapour pressure resinous base gives the pair a time structure of its own: the flower for the first hours, the amber for the rest. That is a pyramid built across two bottles, and it is why a Fragrantica advice column recommends a plain cologne as an uplift to something darker and heavier underneath. The heavier-first order is the one practitioners give (CaFleureBon 2021).
2
Day one: read for dominance at three hours
3:00

Which of the two is in charge now? The prediction was made about this moment.

Watch for: Liking either one aloneNeither held your attention on its own. That is not the test here and it should not colour the reading.
3
Day two: the relay

V Amber Fouguere alone in the morning. At hour three, when it has settled into frankincense and amber, add Fleur d'Oranger 27 above it. Read at 3:30 and 6:00.

Why a relay is differentA German enthusiast blogger describes a relay effect, spraying a complementary scent onto the fading drydown of the first rather than simultaneously, as working better than stacking two full compositions (Parfumo, November 2024); the Fragrantica column describes the same move for heavy orientals. The mechanism is the clock: at hour three the amber's own volatile materials are gone, so the blossom is landing on a base rather than on a competing opening.
4
Compare the two days

Same two bottles, same doses, different timing. Which day did the pair read as one thing sooner? Which would you wear?

Why this comparison transfersTiming is a layering variable in its own right, alongside order, zone and cloth. A pair that does not hold simultaneously may succeed as a relay, and knowing which of your bottles want a head start is half of composing with them.
D

Someone already made this

Lys Solaberg alone: a lily on a smoky woody base. A professional's version of the pair you built the day before, composed rather than stacked, by a perfumer who keeps her own skin neutral to stay able to judge her work.

1 bottle1 comparison6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Lys Solaberg, two sprays, one forearm, the day after lesson 10.
  • Lesson 10's readings open beside you.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Wine lees, quince and bergamot.Where is the lily? Write when you first find it.
2:00Lily, dried fruit and iris over the first of the base.What does this have that your stack did not?
6:00Ambroxan, mate, oakmoss, tobacco, smoke, oak.How much of this base is your own palette?
C

Steps

1
Read it against yesterday
2:00

Same clock, same questions, and one more: what does the composed version have that your two-bottle version did not?

Why this bottleIts base carries mate, which is in Fuego Futuro, and ambroxan, which is in Trudon II: most of your own palette under a flower. It also carries iris, which appears in nothing you have rated highly. It was made by Nathalie Feisthauer, who says that as a perfumer she wears less and less and keeps her skin neutral, so that she can still evaluate what she makes (CaFleureBon 2021). A composed floral over dark, by someone that careful, is the fastest way to find what stacking cannot reach.
2
Where the flower and the smoke meet

At two hours, try to find the material that joins the lily to the base. It is probably not one you can name; that is the point.

Why a composition joins and a stack does notA perfumer can put a bridge material in the middle of a formula that both halves share, at a ratio she has tested; Carles built every accord as a graded pair from nine to one down to five to five before adding anything else. Two finished bottles side by side have no such middle unless they happen to share a material. That is the edge of layering, and lesson 12 is where you try to put a bridge in by hand.
D

Prediction, then result

Your choiceTwo open bottlesOpen plus open

Your build

Any two open bottles from your own shelf. The prediction is written before the spray, and choosing is the skill. If they refuse to merge, a third bottle that shares a material with both is the bridge, and your own verdicts say which material.

2 bottles, yours1 bridge if needed2 days
A

Before you start

  • Two open bottles of your choosing. Write which, and why, before you spray.
  • For day two if needed: an elemi bottle. Elemi is in four of the seven bottles you rated excellent and in none you rated lower; at home that means Ouranon, Fuego Futuro, Rain Wood and Angelica.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Your openings.As predicted?
2:00Your hearts.Merged, or side by side?
6:00Your drydowns.Gain, loss, wear it? If side by side, plan day two.
C

Steps

1
Choose, and say why

Pick the two. Write one sentence on what you expect the second to do to the first: add a top, add a surface, add a direction the first lacks. The sentence is the lesson.

Why the sentence mattersUp to here the pairs were handed to you, which is why the earlier lessons cannot tell you much about what you have actually picked up. A prediction you wrote yourself, in the vocabulary of role and vapour pressure, can. Sommelier students two months into training could name odours better than controls and could not discriminate them better (Poupon et al. 2019); the naming is what a course installs first, and this is where it shows.
2
If they refuse to merge, bridge on day two

If at two hours you smell two things, a third bottle that shares a material with both can join them. On a second day, put one spray of an elemi bottle in a zone between the two.

Why elemi, and why one sprayA shared material gives two compositions something to meet on; it is the closest a stack gets to a composed middle. Elemi is yours by the evidence of your own sheet. One spray, because three bottles at once is more material, and more material is mud; the bridge is a second experiment, not a rescue of the first.
Watch for: Bridging two bottles that already mergedIf day one read as one thing at two hours, there is nothing to bridge. Day two is only for a side-by-side result.
D

One strong bottleThree daysStrong and composed

Portrait of a Lady, wearable

Three attempts across three days: on a scarf, under a quiet bottle as a relay, and alone at half the dose. Less is not the same as anchored, and this is where you feel the difference on a bottle you own and do not wear.

1 bottle3 days3 operations
A

Before you start

  • Day one: one spray of Portrait of a Lady on a scarf, worn. Nothing on skin.
  • Day two: one spray of Portrait of a Lady on the wrist in the morning; at hour two, one spray of Trudon II a hand's width above it. A relay with a quiet bottle.
  • Day three: half a spray on skin, nothing else. Spray once into the air at chest height and walk through it if a half spray is hard to do.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Rose, clove and raspberry, at whatever distance the day's method puts them.Loud, or present?
3:00Patchouli, incense and sandalwood.Would you leave the flat like this?
6:00Musk, benzoin and amber.Gain, loss, and which day won.
C

Steps

1
Day one: the scarf

One spray on a scarf, worn. The rose is at a distance from your nose and from your skin's warmth.

Why the scarfCloth holds the scent and does not warm it, so the bottle stays itself at a lower volume and a greater distance. This is lesson 7's cuff, used as a tool. Robin at Now Smell This suggests the other version of the same idea for a bottle this strong: decant it so you can apply the teensiest little dab.
2
Day two: a quiet bottle over it, as a relay

One spray of Portrait of a Lady on the wrist. At hour two, one spray of Trudon II a hand's width above it.

Why Trudon II, and why at hour twoTrudon II's base is ambroxan and cashmeran: a quiet, fixative-heavy bottle that adds body without adding much of a smell, which is what you want over something that already has too much to say. At hour two the rose's clove and raspberry have gone and you are putting the green over patchouli and incense, materials Trudon II already shares. This is the relay from lesson 10, run in the other direction: a quiet bottle onto a strong drydown.
Watch for: Putting the strong one on topThe order matters here more than anywhere. Portrait of a Lady over Trudon II is Portrait of a Lady.
3
Day three: half a dose, alone

Half a spray. This is the control for the other two: the bottle itself at a lower volume, with nothing else changed.

Why dose is a separate variableA smaller dose makes a strong scent quieter and leaves its shape intact; a second bottle changes the shape. Both end in something more wearable, and they are not the same operation. Some materials also change character with concentration rather than just volume, indole and the animalic musks most famously, and a strong rose-patchouli at half dose may read as a different perfume, not a quieter one. Day three finds out which.
D

Prediction, then result

Where this splits. The result decides which branch you are on.

One wayIf the half-dose version works, this was a question of amount and the bottle can go back into rotation as it is, applied differently.
The otherIf only the relay works, the rose wants a partner and sits with the open bottles despite its strength, and Trudon II is its partner.

The axis you reject

Boss Bottled Night on the wrist, one of yours above it. The only bottle at home on the mainstream designer axis, and the one operation that separates two possible reasons for rejecting it.

1 designer bottle1 of yours6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Boss Bottled Night, one spray on the left wrist.
  • One of yours, one spray a hand's width up. Pick whichever you think has the best chance and write why before you spray. A shared material is the strongest reason; a contrasting vapour pressure is the second.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Birch leaf and lavender in the air under your bottle's opening.Yours, or theirs with something on top?
2:00Violet, jasmine and cardamom.Has your bottle claimed it, or is it arguing?

Steps

1
Pick the partner and say why

Choose which of yours goes above it, and write the reason before you spray.

Why this lesson existsYour record holds both halves of the tension already: you notice and admire mainstream scents on other people, and you never wear them. A rejection can be of the materials or of the way they are put together. Layering changes the construction and leaves the materials alone, which makes it a clean test between the two. This bottle also carries violet and cardamom, both of which appear only among the bottles you rated lower, so one candidate answer is already on the table.
2
Read for ownership at two hours
2:00

Is this now a scent of yours with a mainstream base, or a mainstream scent with something odd on top? Those are the two outcomes, and arguing, two things that refuse to settle, is a third worth naming.

Watch for: Judging it as a perfumeYou are not deciding whether you like Boss Bottled Night. You are deciding what your bottle did to it.
D

Prediction, then result

Where this splits. The result decides which branch you are on.

One wayIf the layer claims it, the mainstream axis is material like any other, and much cheaper material than anything else at home.
The otherIf it stays generic under everything you own, the objection is to how it is built rather than to what is in it, and no amount of layering will move that. Either answer is worth having.

Your choiceA full dayStrong and composed

The pair you expect not to work

Two bottles you expect will not go together, worn for a full day, and written up in the vocabulary of why pairs do not hold. The vocabulary is the lesson; the pair is the apparatus.

2 bottles, yours1 post-mortem6 h of readings
A

Before you start

  • Two bottles you expect will not go together. Write the expected outcome before you spray, using one of the four words below.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Whatever it is.Which one was meant to be the base?
2:00Whatever it is now.What did the top take away?
6:00Whatever is left.At which hour did it stop holding together, and which of the four words?
C

Steps

1
The four words

Muddy: too much mid-weight material, nothing on top or underneath, and often a headache. Loud: overlap summing, the same idea at twice the dose. Flat: no spread of vapour pressure, everything leaving at once, so the pair has no clock. Arguing: two constructions that share nothing to meet on and never settle into one thing.

Where the words come fromPractitioners name the same outcomes independently. A natural perfumer warns that two initially heavy fragrances become overpowering and in the end smell muddy and can lead into a headache (CaFleureBon 2021). A German blogger describes results that get overloaded and disharmonious, and citrus lost against dark bases (Parfumo 2024). A reader at Now Smell This reports two perfumes that have not stopped arguing all morning. Each word has a cause, and the cause is what you can fix next time.
2
Three questions, in role terms

Which one was the base. What the top layer took away. At which hour it stopped holding together. Answer all three before you write anything about liking it.

Why the vocabulary of what does not holdNaming why a combination does not hold is the part that transfers. A vocabulary built only on the pairs you liked describes your taste; one that also covers the rest describes the mechanism, and mechanism is what predicts the next pair. Perfumer training works the same way: a nose is defined by Carles as someone who can tell lavender 50 from lavender 40, which is a skill of noticing what is wrong, not what is nice.
D

Prediction, then result

  • Robin, Perfumista tip: on perfume layering, Now Smell This, December 2007

A borrowed bottleTwo zonesAcross families

Fruit over campfire

Smoke and dry wood on the wrist, pear and white musk above. Nothing in your bottles contains fruit and nothing contains a clean white musk, so this is the first pair with no prior at all, and the first that reaches the direction your record says you are chasing.

1 of yours1 borrowed6 h of readings

A borrowed bottle, so ask the owner before each of these two. Jo Malone London, pear over sweet pea on a clean white musk. That base matters as much as the fruit: a white musk is the one thing at home that adds almost no smell of its own, which is a fixative by another name.

A

Before you start

  • Moonlark Ash, one spray on the left wrist. English Pear & Sweet Pea, one spray a hand's width up.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Pear in the air over bergamot and black pepper.Foreign object, or found sweetness?
2:00Sweet pea over pine and tree sap.Is the musk doing anything? Is the smoke quieter or just further away?
6:00White musk over cypress, vetiver and incense.Gain, loss, and the fork.
C

Steps

1
Smoke on the wrist, fruit above

Moonlark Ash first, English Pear & Sweet Pea a minute later.

Why there is no priorEverything up to here has been recombination inside a range you already know well enough to guess at. A fruit and a white musk are outside that range, so the prediction is a real one. Perfumers interviewed about layering name fruity florals over dark and resinous bases as one of the pairings that adds a dimension rather than competing (CaFleureBon 2021); whether that holds for your nose is the question.
2
Read the musk separately at two hours
2:00

Try to separate what the pear is doing from what the musk is doing. The pear is the foreign object; the musk is a quiet fixative that may be holding the whole pair together, or holding the smoke at a distance.

Why the musk is the interesting halfA white musk is close to what lesson 4 tested: low vapour pressure, little character, and the ability to slow everything else down. If the pair reads as one thing, the musk may deserve more of the credit than the pear. Musk perception is receptor-specific and varies by person: about one in twelve could not smell a macrocyclic musk in the 1973 study, a named receptor drives blindness to Galaxolide (PLOS Genetics 2021), and the perfumer Maurice Roucel is reported to be unable to smell Galaxolide while composing with it (Bois de Jasmin 2025). If the musk reads as nothing to you, that is information, not a failure of attention.
D

Prediction, then result

Where this splits. The result decides which branch you are on.

One wayIf it holds, the off-axis direction is reachable from bottles already in the flat and the next thing to buy is a family, not another bottle in the range you own.
The otherIf the fruit refuses to belong, that is a real answer about how narrow the range is, and the search should stay adjacent instead of jumping.
Sources
  • Perfumer workshop: layering natural fragrances, part 1, CaFleureBon, June 2021
  • From musk to body odor: decoding olfaction through genetic variation, PLOS Genetics 2021
  • Whissell-Buechy and Amoore, Odour-blindness to musk: simple recessive inheritance, Nature 1973
  • Victoria Frolova, Why some people smell nothing in Baccarat Rouge 540, Bois de Jasmin, August 2025
A borrowed bottleTwo zonesAcross families

Honey against resin

Resin, hay and frankincense on the wrist; osmanthus and honey above. Sharper than it looks, because Ouranon already carries the closest thing you own to sweetness and you rated it excellent. The pair asks a question about your own record.

1 of yours1 borrowed6 h of readings

A borrowed bottle. Serge Lutens, 2009, Christopher Sheldrake: mandarin and jasmine over osmanthus, lily and carnation, on musk, honey and almond.

A

Before you start

  • Ouranon, one spray on the left wrist. Nuit de Cellophane, one spray a hand's width up.
B

The clock: what to read, and when

Set alarms. A reading taken when you happen to notice the scent over-samples the loud moments.

TimeWhat is happeningWhat to write
0:30Mandarin and jasmine in the air over lavender and elemi.Sweet, or bright?
2:00Osmanthus and honey over hay and camomile.Does the hay hold the honey, or does the honey float?
6:00Almond and musk over myrrh, patchouli and tonka.Gain, loss, and the answer to the record's rule.
C

Steps

1
Resin on the wrist, honey above

Ouranon first, Nuit de Cellophane a minute later.

Why OuranonIt carries tonka bean and hay, which are the closest thing you own to sweetness, and you rated it excellent. It also carries elemi, your documented bridge, and frankincense under the hay. So this pair asks a sharper question than whether you like it: is the rule in your record against sweetness itself, or only against sweetness with nothing under it?
2
Osmanthus, separately
2:00

Osmanthus reads as apricot and leather at the same time. At two hours, try to hear the leather half of it against the hay; that is the material most likely to be doing the joining.

Why osmanthus might be the bridgeA material with two faces can meet two bases. The apricot face meets the honey and the mandarin; the leather face meets the hay and the resin. If this pair reads as one thing, that double-faced material is probably why, and it is a shape worth recognising: the bridge is not always a shared material, sometimes it is one material that faces both ways.
D

Prediction, then result

Sources
  • Perfumer workshop: layering natural fragrances, part 1, CaFleureBon, June 2021
  • Jean Carles, A method of creation in perfumery, 1961 (PDF)
What this teaches, and where it transfers
Calibration 1: a perfume is a process

What a bottle is at 0:30 and what it is at 6:00 are different materials, and most verdicts, including the ones in your sheet, were written on the first. Every later lesson reads a pair at these same clock times. This day is the habit being installed.

Step 2: the clock is the method

Fixed reading times are what make results comparable across seventeen lessons and across bottles. Attention-driven sniffing produces a different, biased dataset every day.

Step 3: adaptation is the main source of wrong conclusions

It is central, not receptor fatigue, and it outlasts the wearing by a long margin (Dalton and Wysocki 1996). A second nose or a left-behind sleeve is the correction, and lesson 4 tests what happens when the material itself is one your receptors may not report.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
Calibration 2: the drydown is the perfume

Most judgments are made in the window where a perfume is least itself. The opening is the few minutes of the most volatile materials; the drydown is most of the day. Reading both bottles at four hours is what makes complete and open mean something you can act on.

Step 2: A, B, A

The working method for the whole course. It is also how noses are trained: Carles had beginners smell contrasting materials first, then materials within one family, always against each other.

Step 3: vapour pressure, not weight

The evaporation order is a continuous curve, and the pyramid is a sketch of it. Lesson 10 uses this deliberately: a high-vapour-pressure bottle over a low one gives a pair a clock of its own.

Step 4: predict before, read blind where you can

The commit-before-spray box in every lesson exists because of Morrot's dyed wine. A prediction written after the fact is a description.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
Calibration 3: reference materials

Most perfumes are built so that no single material is identifiable, which is why they are hard to learn from. These two are the opposite, and they become the reference points the rest of the course is read against. Carles's beginners smelled contrasting materials first, then materials within one family; lesson 2 was the contrast, this is the within-family pair.

Step 1: vocabulary is the unlock

Your record says you are fluent where a domain has a language you can operate through. This lesson builds that language from your own words, one per material, and the course keeps asking for them.

Step 3: transfer

Name it alone, find it in a composition. The move works for any material you can get close to on its own, and it is what separates hearing a perfume from recognising it.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
Calibration 4: fixatives

A fixative adds body and time with almost no smell of its own, and it slows the top notes as much as it holds the base. Whether you can perceive these two molecules decides whether you can use them. That is a fact about your receptors, and worth knowing early.

Step 2: anosmia is not adaptation

Adaptation is temporary, central and exposure-dependent. Anosmia is permanent, genetic and molecule-specific. Retail copy conflates them constantly. Nearly everyone has some blind spot; knowing yours is as useful as knowing what you love.

Step 3: where fixatives return

Lesson 13 tames a strong bottle, and one of the three methods is putting something quiet over it. If you can smell ambroxan, Trudon II is that quiet thing already on your shelf.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: overlap

Two bottles that share most of their materials sum; they do not add. The result is the same idea at a higher concentration, which usually reads as louder rather than deeper. Every later pair is chosen to share less than these two do.

Step 1: zones are the default

Side by side, sharing the air, is the placement every lesson uses unless it says otherwise. It is the practitioners' finding, not the brands', and lesson 7 lets you check it on your own skin.

Step 2: constant total dose

Halving each spray keeps the comparison to a single bottle honest. It also stops the commonest way a pair goes wrong, which is simply too much.

Step 4: gain and loss

Every pair from here on gets the same two-line verdict. A pair with no nameable gain is not worth wearing, however pleasant it is.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: role

A pair works when the two bottles are doing different jobs. One supplies the statement and one supplies the surface it sits on. Same-role pairs get louder; different-role pairs get deeper. This is the first pair in the course chosen for role rather than family.

Step 2: texture versus dilution

The distinction returns in every open-plus-open lesson. It is the difference between a base and a solvent.

Step 3: a pair has a clock too

Two bottles evaporate on two schedules. The pair at six hours is not the pair at two. Lesson 10 builds a pair around exactly this.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: placement

Layering has three placement variables people collapse into one: whether the two share a spot, which goes down first, and whether one is on cloth. Each changes the result on its own. Run them side by side once and you will not confuse them again.

Step 1: the same-spot test

The brands say stack; the practitioners say zone. Today decides it for your skin. If same-spot wins for you, say so in the record and the later lessons can be run that way.

Step 3: cloth as a tool

Cloth is how you wear a strong bottle at a distance from your own nose. Lesson 13 uses a scarf for exactly this.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: two open bottles

Two bottles that each leave room can fill it for each other, or leave a bigger room. Which happens depends on whether they are open in different directions and whether they share anything to meet on. This is the first pair with no complete bottle to lean on.

Step 2: merged or side by side

The two-perfumes result comes back in every remaining lesson. A shared material, a bridge, is usually what turns side by side into merged. Lesson 12 is where you choose one deliberately.

Step 3: a pair has a clock

Merging late is the norm, not the exception. Naming the hour at which a pair becomes one thing is a better verdict than yes or no.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: direction of openness

Open is not one property. A diffuse bottle and a narrow bottle are both open, but a diffuse one leaves room everywhere and a narrow one leaves room on both sides of a single line. Two narrow bottles on different lines can build; two diffuse ones cannot.

Step 2: when the character is volatile

A bottle whose personality lives in its top is a different layering partner at 0:30 and at 2:00. Match the reading time to where the bottle keeps its character.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: vapour pressure, and timing

A fast bottle over a slow one gives the pair a clock. The fast one is the opening and the slow one is the drydown, which is how a single perfume is built too. This is the layering move most likely to work between any two bottles you own, and the relay is its second form.

Step 1: slow one first

The rule generalises: the slower-evaporating bottle goes down first, the faster one above. It is the same reason a perfumer puts musks in the base and citrus at the top.

Step 3: the relay

Spraying onto a drydown is a different technique from stacking two openings. Lesson 13 uses it to tame a strong bottle.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The limit: composed versus stacked

Layering puts two evaporation curves next to each other; composition weaves one. A perfumer can put a bridge material in the middle that both halves share. You mostly cannot. Knowing exactly what that gap feels like is what stops you chasing it.

Step 2: the bridge

Carles's graded pairs are what a bridge is at the formula level. At the bottle level your only bridge is a shared material, and your own verdicts say which one: elemi.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The skill: prediction

Being able to say what the second bottle will do to the first, and being right more often than not, is the whole course. This is the first lesson that measures it, because it is the first where nothing was given.

Step 2: the bridge

A shared material is what turns two perfumes into one. Elemi is yours by your own verdicts; other people's bridges are musks and ambroxan, which lesson 4 tested.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The variable: dose versus structure

A smaller dose makes a strong scent quieter and leaves its shape intact; putting something over it changes the shape. Two different operations, easy to confuse, because both end in something more wearable. Three days separate them on a bottle you paid for and do not wear.

Step 2: fixatives as tamers

A quiet fixative-heavy bottle over a loud one is what a musk over a loud floral does in enthusiast lore. Trudon II is the version already on your shelf, if lesson 4 said you can smell ambroxan.

Step 3: concentration changes character

Not only volume. This is the mechanism behind lesson 14 too: what you reject in a bottle may be a concentration, not a material.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The question: materials or construction

A rejection can be of the materials or of the way they are put together. Layering changes the construction and leaves the materials alone, which makes it the cleanest test between the two that exists outside a laboratory.

Step 2: three outcomes, not two

Claimed, unclaimed, and arguing. The third is a real result and it has a cause: two constructions that share no material to meet on.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
The vocabulary: muddy, loud, flat, arguing

Four ways a pair stops holding together, and each has a cause. Muddy is too much mid-weight material. Loud is overlap summing. Flat is no vapour-pressure spread. Arguing is no shared material. Naming which is what lets you fix the next one.

Step 2: role, then clock, then liking

The order of the three questions is the order of the whole course. Liking last, because it is the least reusable.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
Across a family line

Material from outside your range tests the range itself. The direction your record says you are chasing, off-axis but lovable, is either reachable from the flat or it is not. This is the cheapest way to find out.

Step 2: the musk is a fixative

Clean white musk over a loud base is enthusiast lore for taming. Here it arrives inside someone else's bottle, doing that job whether or not you asked it to.

What this teaches, and where it transfers
A question about your own record

Not sweet is in your palette as a rule. Ouranon is evidence the rule has an exception when the sweetness has resin under it. This pair pushes on exactly that exception, with a sweetness you have never worn over a resin you love.

Step 2: a two-faced material as a bridge

Lesson 12's bridge was a shared material. This is the other kind: one material with two characters, each meeting a different half. Osmanthus, iris and some musks all do it.
